Natural Language Processing - Twitter Analysis

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

With 330 million monthly active users, Twitter enables businesses to reach a wide audience and engage directly with customers. However, the volume of information makes it challenging for brands to quickly identify negative mentions that could impact their reputation.

As a result, sentiment analysis, which monitors emotions in social media conversations, has become an essential strategy in social media marketing.

Monitoring customer sentiment on Twitter helps companies understand their audience, stay informed about brand and competitor discussions, and identify emerging industry trends.

Objective¶

This project focuses on analyzing customer tweets about U.S. airlines and categorizing their sentiments as positive, neutral, or negative.

Data Description¶

A sentiment analysis job about the problems of each major U.S. airline. Twitter data was scraped from February of 2015 and contributors were asked to first classify positive, negative, and neutral tweets, followed by categorizing negative reasons (such as "late flight" or "rude service").

Data Dictionary¶

  • tweet_id - A unique identifier for each tweet
  • airline_sentiment - The sentiment label of the tweet, such as positive, negative, or neutral
  • airline_sentiment_confidence - The confidence level associated with the sentiment label
  • negativereason - A category indicating the reason for negative sentiment
  • negativereason_confidence - The confidence level associated with the negative reason
  • airline - The airline associated with the tweet
  • airline_sentiment_gold - Gold standard sentiment label
  • name - The username of the tweet author
  • negativereason_gold - Corrected gold standard label for the reason behind a negative tweet
  • retweet_count - The number of times the tweet has been retweeted
  • text - The actual text content of the tweet.
  • tweet_coord - Coordinates of the tweet
  • tweet_created - The timestamp when the tweet was created
  • tweet_location - The location mentioned in the tweet
  • user_timezone - The timezone of the tweet author

Data Preparation for Modeling¶

  • Remove html tags
  • Replace contractions in string(e.g. replace I'm --> I am) and so on.
  • Remove numbers
  • Tokenization
  • To remove Stopwords
  • Lemmatized data
In [20]:
def preprocess_text(text):
    # a. HTML tag removal
    text = BeautifulSoup(text, "html.parser").get_text()
    text = re.sub(r'\d+', '', text)
    
    # c. Remove numbers
    text = re.sub(r'\d+', '', text)
    
    # d. Remove special characters and punctuations
    text = re.sub(r'[^\w\s]', '', text)
    
    # f. Convert to lowercase
    text = text.lower()
    
    # b. Tokenization
    tokens = word_tokenize(text)
    
    # e. Remove stopwords
    stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))
    tokens = [word for word in tokens if word not in stop_words]
    
    # g. Lemmatization
    lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
    tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(word) for word in tokens]
    
    # h. Join tokens back to text
    return " ".join(tokens)

Model Building using countvectorizer¶

  • Intialize countvectorizer and use it for vectorization
  • Store Independent and Dependent variables
  • Split the data into train and test
  • Build a Random Forest model on train data
  • Use Cross validation to validate the score and to find optimal n_estimators
  • Plot the misclassification error for each of estimators
  • Test the model on testing data
  • Plot the Confusion matrix
  • Plot word cloud for top 20 important features obtained from Count vectorizer and random forest model
In [22]:
# Initialize CountVectorizer and vectorize text
count_vec = CountVectorizer(max_features=2000)

# Store Independent and Dependent  variables
X = count_vec.fit_transform(df_model['clean_text']).toarray()  # Independent variable
y = df_model['airline_sentiment']  # Dependent variable
targets = sorted(y.unique().tolist())

# Split the data into train and test
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, shuffle=True)

# Build a Random Forest model on train data (default n_estimators)
rf_default = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
rf_default.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Random Forest trained on training data with default n_estimators")

Random Forest trained on training data with default n_estimators
In [23]:
#Cross Validation to validate score and find optimal n_estimators
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
estimators = [100, 200, 300]
cv_scores = []

for n in estimators:
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n, random_state=42)
    scores = cross_val_score(rf, X_train, y_train, cv=skf, scoring='accuracy')
    cv_scores.append(scores.mean())
In [24]:
# Misclassification error
misclassification_error = [1 - score for score in cv_scores]
plt.figure(figsize=(8,5))
plt.plot(estimators, misclassification_error, marker='o', linestyle='--', color='b')
for i, txt in enumerate(misclassification_error):
    plt.annotate(f"{txt:.3f}", (estimators[i], misclassification_error[i]), 
                 textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0,10), ha='center')
plt.xlabel("Number of Estimators")
plt.ylabel("Misclassification Error")
plt.title("Misclassification Error vs n_estimators")
plt.grid(True)
plt.show()
In [25]:
# Train RandomForest with optimal n_estimators
optimal_n = estimators[np.argmax(cv_scores)]
print(f"Optimal n_estimators: {optimal_n}")

rf_model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=optimal_n, random_state=42)
rf_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

Optimal n_estimators: 200

Using TF-IDF (Term Frequency- Inverse Document Frequency)¶

  • Intialize TFIDF and use it for vectorization
  • Store Independent and Dependent variables
  • Split the data into train and test
  • Build a Random Forest model on train data
  • Use Cross validation to validate the score and to find optimal n_estimators
  • Plot the misclassification error for each of estimators
  • Test the model on testing data
  • Plot the Confusion matrix plot word cloud for top 20 important features obtained from TFIDF and random forest model
In [30]:
# Initialize TF-IDF and use it for vectorization
tfidf_vec = TfidfVectorizer(max_features=2000)
X_tfidf = tfidf_vec.fit_transform(df_model['clean_text']).toarray()

# Store Independent and Dependent variables
X = X_tfidf   # Independent variable
y = df_model['airline_sentiment'].reset_index(drop=True)  # Dependent variable
targets = sorted(y.unique().tolist())

# Split the data into train and test
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, shuffle=True)

# Build a Random Forest model on train data (default n_estimators)
rf_default = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
rf_default.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Random Forest trained on training data with default n_estimators")

Random Forest trained on training data with default n_estimators
In [ ]:
# Cross validation to validate the score and find optimal n_estimators
skf = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=42)
estimators = [100, 200,300,400]
cv_scores = []

for n in estimators:
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n, random_state=42)
    scores = cross_val_score(rf, X_train, y_train, cv=skf, scoring='accuracy')
    cv_scores.append(scores.mean())

# Find the best estimator
optimal_n = estimators[np.argmax(cv_scores)]
print(f"Optimal n_estimators = {optimal_n}")

# Plot the misclassification error for each of estimators
errors = [1 - score for score in cv_scores]
plt.plot(estimators, errors, marker='o', linestyle='--', color='r')
for i, err in enumerate(errors):

                 textcoords="offset points", xytext=(0,10), ha='center')
plt.xlabel("n_estimators")
plt.ylabel("Misclassification Error (1 - Accuracy)")
plt.title("Misclassification Error vs n_estimators (TF-IDF + RF)")

  • Using TF-IDF, some of the top 20 important features for the Random Forest model include words such as jetblue, thank, united, southwestair, great, cancelled, etc. These words strongly indicate sentiment: complaint-related words like cancelled contribute to negative predictions, while words like thank signal positive sentiment.

Summary of Airline Sentiment Analysis¶

  • Pre-processing:

    • Cleaning tweets reduced noise and highlighted sentiment bearing words like delay, cancelled, great, love.

  • Vectorization & Modeling:

    • CountVectorizer and TF-IDF converted text into numeric features for Random Forest.

    • Cross-validation helped select optimal number of trees, stabilizing performance.

  • Model Performance:

    • Best accuracy achieved for negative tweets (94%), moderate for positive (62%), and lowest for neutral (40%).

    • Neutral tweets were hardest to classify due to overlapping wording with other sentiments.

  • Feature Insights:

    • Confusion matrix showed misclassifications mostly between neutral and negative tweets.

    • Top features (via word cloud) reflected meaningful sentiment words: negative tweets included delay, cancelled, baggage; positive tweets included thanks, great, love.

  • Business Implications:

    • TF-IDF + Random Forest achieved slightly higher overall accuracy and performed best for negative tweets, while CountVectorizer + Random Forest performed better for neutral and positive tweets.

    • Airlines can rapidly detect negative sentiment and respond proactively.Airlines can identify parts of customer experience driving sentiment and react faster to negative tweets, improving customer satisfaction and reducing potential business impact.
